title: Projective Algebraic Sets Projective Morphisms and Cones

items.title: Projective n-space as proportional nonzero vectors
Homogeneous polynomials and homogeneous ideals
A homogeneous polynomial has a well-defined projective zero locus
items.strategy: For a degree-d form F, replace a nonzero representative a by lambda a and use F(lambda a)=lambda^d F(a). Since lambda is nonzero, the two values vanish simultaneously; state the degree-zero boundary explicitly.

items.title: Projective algebraic sets and the irrelevant ideal
Homogeneous zero loci define the projective Zariski topology
items.strategy: Use unions of families of homogeneous equations for arbitrary intersections and products of homogeneous ideals for finite unions. Treat V_+(0), V_+((x_0,...,x_n)), and the standard complements D_+(x_i) explicitly so the irrelevant-ideal boundary is not hidden.

items.title: Every standard projective open is an affine n-space
items.strategy: On D_+(x_i), normalize the i-th homogeneous coordinate to one and map to the remaining ratios x_j/x_i. Write the inverse by inserting 1 in position i, then verify both composites and the Zariski-topology correspondence by homogenizing and dehomogenizing equations.

items.title: Homogenization, dehomogenization, and saturation agree on the x_0-chart
items.strategy: Define f^h by clearing the largest x_0-power after f(x_1/x_0,...,x_n/x_0), and dehomogenize by x_0=1. For I=(f_1,...,f_r), compare the all-polynomial homogenization I^h with J=(f_1^h,...,f_r^h) after inverting x_0, then clear a power of x_0 to prove I^h=J:x_0^infinity.

items.title: The projective closure of an affine algebraic set
The ideal of a projective closure is the saturated homogenization ideal
items.strategy: For A=V(I) in the x_0-chart and I=(f_1,...,f_r), use the chart correspondence to identify the closure with V_+(I^h). The preceding lemma rewrites I^h as (f_1^h,...,f_r^h):x_0^infinity; use the projective Nullstellensatz correspondence to identify this saturated homogeneous ideal with I_+(closure A).

items.title: The homogeneous coordinate ring of a projective algebraic set
A classical projective variety
Projective irreducibility and the homogeneous prime ideal
items.strategy: Pass between a nonempty projective algebraic set and its affine cone. Apply the affine radical/prime correspondence to the cone, and exclude the irrelevant ideal so that the empty projective locus is not mistaken for a variety.

items.title: Regular functions on a classical projective variety
Degree-zero projective quotients agree with affine-chart regularity
items.strategy: On D_+(x_i), divide equal-degree homogeneous numerator and denominator by the same power of x_i. The quotient becomes an ordinary rational expression in affine ratios, and the transition x_j/x_i=(x_j/x_l)/(x_i/x_l) proves agreement on overlaps in both directions.

items.title: Global regular functions on a classical projective variety are constant
items.strategy: Work over the established algebraically closed base field and use the degree-zero homogeneous-quotient description on the standard affine charts. A global regular quotient has no pole along every homogeneous divisor; the elementary homogeneous argument forces its numerator to be a scalar multiple of its denominator. Do not invoke properness, which is built later.

items.title: Morphisms to projective space from homogeneous coordinate tuples
Homogeneous-coordinate morphisms are well defined and glue on target charts
items.strategy: Equal source degree makes rescaling a source representative rescale every target coordinate by one common scalar. On the open where F_i is nonzero, the target affine coordinates are F_j/F_i; chart compatibility makes these regular and their overlap formulas agree.

items.title: A homogeneous coordinate surjection presents a closed projective embedding
items.strategy: For a chosen projective embedding, identify the homogeneous coordinate ring as a quotient of a polynomial ring by its homogeneous vanishing ideal. Conversely, a degree-preserving surjection from a polynomial ring has homogeneous kernel; its projective zero locus is the image, and the standard-chart quotient maps give the inverse local coordinate-ring description.

items.title: The affine cone over a projective algebraic set
A projective variety and its affine cone have the same irreducibility condition
items.strategy: The cone of V_+(I) has vanishing ideal I_+(V_+(I)), including the vertex. Apply the affine prime/irreducible correspondence and the preceding projective prime criterion; explicitly exclude the irrelevant ideal and the empty locus.

items.title: The affine chart is dense in its projective closure
items.strategy: Use the definition of projective closure to obtain density, then use dehomogenization to identify its intersection with D_+(x_0) with the original affine algebraic set. State separately that the no-component-at-infinity condition is what permits recovery of a given projective set from this chart; it is not needed to make a set dense in its own closure.

items.title: The degree of a projective hypersurface
Affine pieces and transition functions of a projective hypersurface
items.strategy: On D_+(x_i), divide the defining degree-d form by x_i^d to obtain its dehomogenization. On overlaps substitute the ratio coordinates into one another and use homogeneity to show that the two equations cut out the same localized affine coordinate ring.

items.title: The homogeneous coordinate ring is not a ring of scalar-valued global functions

title: Projective Algebraic Sets Projective Morphisms and Cones — Examples

items.title: The two affine charts of the projective line
items.strategy: Use t=x_1/x_0 on D_+(x_0) and u=x_0/x_1 on D_+(x_1). On their intersection compute tu=1, then identify t=0 and u=0 as the two distinguished chart points usually called zero and infinity.

items.title: The projective closure of the parabola y=x^2
items.strategy: Homogenize y-x^2 to x_0x_2-x_1^2 in coordinates [x_0:x_1:x_2]. Dehomogenize on x_0 not equal to zero to recover the affine parabola, and set x_0=0 to obtain its unique point at infinity [0:0:1].

items.title: Homogenizing a chosen generating set can add a component at infinity
items.strategy: For I=(x_2-x_1^2,x_3-x_1^3), compare the raw homogenized-generator ideal (x_0x_2-x_1^2,x_0^2x_3-x_1^3) with its x_0-saturation. At x_0=0 the raw ideal contains an extra projective line, while saturation adds the missing relation x_1x_3-x_2^2 and leaves only the true point at infinity.

items.title: Standard affine charts of the conic XZ=Y^2
items.strategy: Dehomogenize XZ-Y^2 on the X, Y, and Z charts. The first and third charts are affine parabolas z=y^2 and x=y^2, while the middle chart is the hyperbola xz=1; compute the ratio-coordinate transitions on overlaps.

items.title: The affine cone over a smooth projective conic has a singular vertex
items.strategy: Assume char(k) is not 2. For X=V_+(XZ-Y^2) in P^2, compute its affine cone V(xz-y^2) in A^3. The displayed partial derivatives show that the projective conic has no singular projective point whereas all first derivatives vanish at the cone vertex, making the contrast explicit without invoking the later general smoothness theory.

items.title: An inhomogeneous equation does not descend to projective space
items.strategy: In P^1, the nonzero vector (-1,0) satisfies the inhomogeneous expression x_0+1=0, but its proportional representative (-2,0) does not. This directly shows why a projective equation must be homogeneous.

items.title: The degree-d power map of the projective line
items.strategy: For d at least 1, use [s:t] maps to [s^d:t^d] and verify no common zero and common degree. On the standard affine coordinate it is u maps to u^d; describe the generic d-point fibre when char(k) does not divide d and the inseparable p-power behavior when d has characteristic-p factors.
